Lady
lā´dĭ
n. (a woman of rank; in Isaiah, a title Babylon claimed — Hebrew gebereth; Greek kuria)
Old English hlæfdige, literally the loaf-kneader, the mistress of a household who distributed the bread. The Hebrew gebereth is a mistress or ruling woman; the Greek kuria is the feminine of kurios, lord.

Biblical Definition

Lady appears in the Authorized Version in two settings that could hardly be further apart. Isaiah addresses Babylon by the title she had taken: “Sit thou silent, and get thee into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called, The lady of kingdoms” (Isa 47:5), and names the presumption underneath it: “And thou saidst, I shall be a lady for ever: so that thou didst not lay these things to thy heart, neither didst remember the latter end of it” (Isa 47:7). Permanence assumed and the latter end unconsidered — that is the whole indictment of empires in one line. The other use is John's greeting: “The elder unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth; and not I only, but also all they that have known the truth” (2Jn 1:1), and “now I beseech thee, lady, not as though I wrote a new commandment unto thee, but that which we had from the beginning, that we love one another” (2Jn 1:5). An aged apostle writes a short letter to a Christian woman — or to a congregation addressed under that figure — about walking in truth, loving one another, and refusing hospitality to men who bring another doctrine. The lady of kingdoms is silenced; the elect lady is loved in the truth by all who know the truth.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a lady as a woman of distinction; a title given to the wives of knights and of all degrees above them; and, in common usage, a well bred woman.

expand to see more

LA'DY, n. A woman of distinction. Originally, the title was given to the daughters of earls and others in high rank, but it is now given to any well bred woman.

2. A word of complaisance; a well bred woman.

3. Mistress; the female who presides or has authority over a family or household.

MIS'TRESS, n. A woman who governs; correlative to servant or slave; the female head of a family.

Key Scripture

2 John 1:1 — "The elder unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth; and not I only, but also all they that have known the truth;"

2 John 1:5 — "And now I beseech thee, lady, not as though I wrote a new commandment unto thee, but that which we had from the beginning, that we love one another."

Isaiah 47:5 — "Sit thou silent, and get thee into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called, The lady of kingdoms."

Isaiah 47:7 — "And thou saidst, I shall be a lady for ever: so that thou didst not lay these things to thy heart, neither didst remember the latter end of it."

Modern Corruption

Love and truth are set against each other, when the shortest letter in the New Testament joins them in every paragraph and then bars the door to false teachers.

expand to see more

Second John is four hundred words long and it says truth five times and love four, and never once sets them at odds. John loves the elect lady in the truth; he rejoices that her children walk in truth; he beseeches her that they love one another; and in the same breath he forbids her to receive into her house, or to bid God speed, anyone who brings not the doctrine of Christ. That last instruction is unbearable to a generation taught that love means unlimited welcome, and it comes from the apostle whom that same generation quotes on love. The letter is the standing proof that Christian love has a doctrinal shape and a door it will not open.

Isaiah 47 shows the other lady and her ruin. Babylon called herself the lady of kingdoms and said in her heart, I shall be a lady for ever, and the prophet fastens on what that boast made her stop doing: she did not lay these things to her heart, neither did she remember the latter end. Assumed permanence produces unconsidered ends, in an empire and in a soul. The remedy Moses prayed for is exactly the opposite: teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gebereth (H1404), mistress, lady — Isaiah 47:5, 47:7, Genesis 16:4 of Sarai; Greek kuria (G2959), lady — 2 John 1:1, 1:5, the feminine of kurios.

expand to see more

Hebrew gebereth (H1404) — mistress, lady; Isaiah 47:5 and 47:7, Genesis 16:4, 1 Kings 11:19.

Greek kuria (G2959) — lady, the feminine of lord; 2 John 1:1 and 1:5, its only occurrences.

Greek eklektos (G1588) — elect, chosen; the adjective John attaches to her, and to her sister in verse 13.

Old English hlæfdige, the loaf-kneader — the mistress who distributed the household bread.

2 John 10 gives the letter's hard clause: receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed.

Usage

"“The elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth”."

"“I shall be a lady for ever” — and the latter end unremembered."

"Love in the truth, and a door not opened to another doctrine."
